prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
High-quality text-to-image generative models are increasingly being exploited to generate massive amounts of synthetic data. A critical, unaddressed security gap exists where unauthorized parties use this synthetic data to train downstream discriminative models (e.g., image classifiers) rather than competing generative models. Current intellectual property protection methods, such as watermarking or generative artifacts analysis, fail in this scenario because the suspect model performs a completely different task (classification vs. generation) and the defender often has only black-box API access to the suspect model. We lack a mechanism to verify if a third-party classifier was trained on synthetic data derived from our proprietary generative model.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the provenance of training data can be inferred through the principle of **generalization error alignment**. Our central hypothesis is that if two models are trained for the same task using data from the same underlying distribution (i.e., the same generative source), their generalization behaviors (performance patterns and error rates) on a validation set drawn from that same source will be statistically similar. Conversely, if the suspect model was trained on real data or data from a different generator, its performance on our specific synthetic validation set will diverge significantly from a model known to be trained on our data.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a "Training Data Provenance Verification" framework that operates without needing access to the suspect model's weights or gradients. The approach utilizes a "Shadow Modeling" strategy:

1.  **Synthetic Proxy Generation:**
    Using our proprietary generative model, we will synthesize two distinct datasets tailored to the target task of the suspect model:
    *   A **Shadow Training Set** to simulate the suspect's potential training data.
    *   A **Validation Set** to serve as the probe for verification.

2.  **Shadow Model Training:**
    We will train a local "Shadow Model" using the Shadow Training Set. This model acts as a ground-truth reference, representing how a model *should* behave if it were indeed trained on our synthetic data.

3.  **Black-Box Comparative Inference:**
    We will feed the generated Validation Set into both the local Shadow Model and the remote Suspect Model (via API). We will record the prediction outputs (labels or confidence scores) for both.

4.  **Statistical Hypothesis Testing:**
    We will employ a statistical test (e.g., a one-sided outlier test) to compare the performance distributions of the two models.
    *   The system will measure the discrepancy between the Suspect Model's accuracy and the Shadow Model's accuracy on the specific validation samples.
    *   If the Suspect Model's performance profile closely aligns with the Shadow Model (falling within a statistically expected range), we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the Suspect Model likely utilized our synthetic data.

## Expected Contribution
This project aims to establish the first viable defense against the unauthorized use of synthetic data for training downstream discriminative tasks. By validating the link between data distribution sources and generalization error bounds, we expect to provide a robust, black-box verification tool for model owners. This will enable intellectual property protection in "Machine Learning as a Service" (MLaaS) scenarios where defenders cannot inspect the internal architecture of suspicious models.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive framework to verify if a suspect model ($M_{sus}$) was trained on synthetic data generated by a specific defender's generative model ($G_d$). The experiments were conducted in a black-box setting where the defender only had access to the prediction API (labels) of the suspect model.

### Datasets and Generative Models
*   **Visual Datasets (Real):** CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet-100 (a random subset of ImageNet-1K with 100 categories and 126,689 images).
*   **Text-to-Image Models ($G_d$):** Stable Diffusion v1.4, Latent Consistency Model, PixArt-$\alpha$, Stable Cascade.
*   **Synthetic Datasets:** To distinguish from real datasets, synthetic versions were denoted as CIFAR10-Syn, CIFAR100-Syn, and ImageNet-100-Syn.

### Shadow and Validation Dataset Generation ($D_{sdw}$ & $D_v$)
We used the defender's model ($G_d$) to generate data.
*   **CIFAR Settings:**
    *   **Shadow Dataset ($D_{sdw}$):** 30,000 images, resolution $32 \times 32$. Text prompt: "a {c}".
    *   **Validation Dataset ($D_v$):** 5,000 images, resolution $32 \times 32$. Text prompt: "a photo of a {c}".
*   **ImageNet-100 Settings:**
    *   **Shadow Dataset ($D_{sdw}$):** 50,000 images, resolution $256 \times 256$.
    *   **Validation Dataset ($D_v$):** 5,000 images, resolution $256 \times 256$.

### Shadow Model Training ($M_{sdw}$)
*   **Architecture:** ResNet18 (default). Also tested ConvNeXt-B and Swin-B for ablation.
*   **Optimizer:** SGD (implied by weight decay/momentum context, though text specifies hyperparameters).
*   **Learning Rate:** 1e-4.
*   **Weight Decay:** 0.9.
*   **Loss Function:** Cross-entropy loss.
*   **Training Epochs:** 100 (default).
*   **Batch Size:** 512 (CIFAR), 64 (ImageNet-100).

### Suspect Model Simulation ($M_{sus}$)
To simulate various real-world scenarios, we trained a diverse set of suspect models.
*   **Training Data Volume:** 60,000 images (CIFAR-Syn), 100,000 images (ImageNet-100-Syn).
*   **Architectures:** ResNet50, ResNet101, ViT-S/16, ViT-B/16.
*   **Training Hyperparameters:**
    *   Batch Sizes: 512 or 256 (CIFAR); 64 or 32 (ImageNet-100).
    *   Learning Rates: 1e-4 or 5e-5.
    *   Weight Decay: 0.9 or 0.09.
    *   Loss Functions: Cross-entropy loss or Focal loss.
*   **Total Suspect Models:** 64 distinct models per dataset type ($C_4^1 \times C_2^1 \times C_2^1 \times C_2^1 \times C_2^1$).
*   **Inference Batch Size:** 128 (CIFAR), 16 (ImageNet-100).

### Baselines Compared
1.  **Random Classification:** Randomly classifying suspicious models as illegal or legal.
2.  **Attribution Baseline (Han et al.):** Trains an attributor using multiple generative models. (Note: In our evaluation, we relaxed constraints to allow this baseline access to all four text-to-image models).
3.  **TrainProVe-Ent:** Hypothesis testing based on the entropy of predicted logits.
4.  **TrainProVe-Sim:** Hypothesis testing based on pairwise cosine similarity of logits within the same category.

### Evaluation Metrics
The task was a binary classification of $M_{sus}$ as **Illegal** (trained on $G_d$ data) or **Legal** (trained on other sources).
*   **Metrics:** Accuracy, F1 Score, AUROC.
*   **Hypothesis Test:** One-sided Grubbs’ hypothesis test on the prediction accuracy of $M_{sus}$ and $M_{sdw}$ on $D_v$.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Observations from Figure 4 (Impact of Training Epochs on $M_{sdw}$)**
*   We tracked Average Accuracy, F1, and AUROC while varying $M_{sdw}$ training epochs from 20 to 200 (CIFAR10).
*   **Accuracy:** Started at 0.946 (epoch 20), rose to 0.988 (epoch 40), stabilized between 0.996 and 0.998 for epochs 60 through 180, and dropped to 0.895 at epoch 200.
*   **F1 Score:** Started at 0.946 (epoch 20), rose to 0.97 (epoch 40), stabilized between 0.99 and 0.994 for epochs 60 through 180, and dropped to 0.859 at epoch 200.
*   **AUROC:** Started at 0.946 (epoch 20), rose to 0.992 (epoch 40), stabilized near 0.998 for epochs 60 through 180, and dropped to 0.934 at epoch 200.
*   **Conclusion:** The method exhibited resilience to epoch variations between 60 and 180. Excessive epochs (200) caused overfitting, and insufficient epochs (20) caused underfitting, both degrading performance.

**Observations from Figure 5 (Impact of Sample Sizes)**
*   We analyzed performance when varying the sample sizes of the shadow dataset ($D_{sdw}$) and validation dataset ($D_v$).
*   The results indicated that TrainProVe generally maintained robustness across different sample sizes.
*   Performance degradation was observed specifically when the sample size of $D_{sdw}$ was too small, which impaired the generalization performance of $M_{sdw}$ on $D_v$.

**Observations from Method Comparisons**
*   TrainProVe consistently outperformed Han et al.'s baseline. Han et al.'s method relied on an attributor that tended to overfit to the specific architecture used by the defender during training, leading to failure when the suspect model architecture differed.
*   TrainProVe outperformed entropy-based (TrainProVe-Ent) and similarity-based (TrainProVe-Sim) baselines. These baselines failed to utilize the true labels for accuracy comparison, resulting in inferior validation performance compared to the proposed method which directly compared generalization errors (accuracies).

**Efficiency Observations**
*   TrainProVe demonstrated significantly higher efficiency than the baseline (Han et al.). TrainProVe required generating only one shadow dataset and training one shadow model.
*   In contrast, the baseline required generating $m$ datasets and training $m \times n$ models (where $m$ is the number of accessible generative models and $n$ is the number of models trained per dataset) to train the attributor.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The proliferation of high-quality, open-source text-to-image diffusion models has significantly lowered the barrier for generating photorealistic synthetic data. While this enables legitimate creativity, it introduces a critical security vulnerability: unauthorized parties may utilize synthetic data generated by our proprietary models to train their own models for specific downstream tasks (e.g., image classification) without permission.

We identify this as a "Case 3" infringement scenario, distinct from direct model theft or knowledge distillation for image generation. In this scenario, the suspect steals synthetic data to train a model for a *different* task. Existing defense mechanisms, such as watermarking or training data attribution, generally rely on identifying distributions of generated images or generative behavior. These methods fail here because the suspect model is a discriminative model (e.g., a classifier), not a generator. Furthermore, we must operate in a black-box setting (Machine Learning as a Service - MLaaS), where we have no access to the suspect model's weights, gradients, or training configurations, and can only observe prediction labels via an API. There is currently no effective method to verify the data provenance of such downstream models.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a novel framework called **Training data Provenance Verification (TrainProVe)**. Our core hypothesis is grounded in the principle of **generalization error bounds**. We posit that if two models are trained for the same task, their generalization capabilities on a specific target domain will be highly similar if and only if their training data distributions are statistically close.

Specifically, if a suspect model ($M_{sus}$) was trained on data synthesized by our generative model ($G_d$), its performance on a validation set generated by $G_d$ will statistically match the performance of a "shadow model" ($M_{sdw}$) that we knowingly train on that same synthetic distribution. Conversely, if $M_{sus}$ was trained on a different source (real data or a different generator), its generalization error on our synthetic validation set will diverge significantly from that of the shadow model. We hypothesize that we can detect this divergence using statistical hypothesis testing on batch-wise prediction accuracies.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct the TrainProVe framework comprising three distinct stages: Dataset Generation, Shadow Model Training, and Hypothesis Testing via Generalization Error Analysis.

### 1. Theoretical Formulation
We define the domain as a feature space $\mathcal{X}$ and a marginal probability distribution $P(\pmb{x})$. Let the defender's generative model be $G_d$. The suspect model $M$ is trained on a source domain $S$ with distribution $P_S(\pmb{x})$.
We rely on the theorem that the difference in generalization error between two models is bounded by the divergence of their source domains. Let $M$ be the model trained on our synthetic data ($P(\pmb{x}|G, \mathcal{T}_1)$) and $\hat{M}$ be the suspect model. We formulate the relationship regarding the generalization error difference $\Delta \epsilon_T$ on a target domain $T$ as follows:

$$ \operatorname* { sup } _ { P _ { 2 } ( \pmb { x } ) = P ( \pmb { x } | G , \mathcal { T } _ { 2 } ) } | \Delta \epsilon _ { T } | \leq \operatorname* { sup } _ { P _ { 2 } ( \pmb { x } ) \bot G } | \Delta \epsilon _ { T } | $$

Where:
*   $\Delta \epsilon _ { T } = \epsilon _ { T } ( M ) - \epsilon _ { T } ( \hat { M } )$ is the difference in generalization error on target domain $T$.
*   $P_2(\pmb{x})$ is the training distribution of the suspect model.
*   $P_2(\pmb{x}) \bot G$ indicates the suspect's data is independent of our generator $G$.
*   $\mathcal{T}$ represents sets of text prompts.

We will operationalize this inequality to distinguish between models trained on our data (LHS) and models trained on unrelated data (RHS).

### 2. Shadow and Validation Dataset Generation
We will utilize our proprietary generator $G_d$ to construct two distinct datasets tailored to the task of the suspect model (e.g., $K$-way classification with label set $\mathcal{C}$):

1.  **Shadow Dataset ($\mathcal{D}_{sdw}$):** Generated using a prompt set $\mathcal{T}_{sdw}$ derived from the label set $\mathcal{C}$. This dataset simulates the "stolen" data distribution.
2.  **Validation Dataset ($\mathcal{D}_{v}$):** Generated using a distinct prompt set $\mathcal{T}_{v}$. This serves as the target domain $T$ for measuring generalization error.

### 3. Shadow Model Training
We will train a white-box proxy model, the **Shadow Model ($M_{sdw}$)**, using the shadow dataset $\mathcal{D}_{sdw}$.
*   **Objective:** To create a benchmark for how a model *should* perform on $\mathcal{D}_{v}$ if it were trained on data from $G_d$.
*   **Configuration:** $M_{sdw}$ will be trained for the same classification task as $M_{sus}$.

### 4. Hypothesis Testing Mechanism
To verify provenance, we will feed the validation dataset $\mathcal{D}_{v}$ into both the black-box suspect model $M_{sus}$ and our shadow model $M_{sdw}$ batch by batch.

1.  **Accuracy Sampling:** We will compute the accuracy for each batch, resulting in two sets of accuracy metrics:
    *   $\mathcal{A}_{sdw}$: The set of batch accuracies for the shadow model.
    *   $\mathcal{A}_{sus}$: The set of batch accuracies for the suspect model.

2.  **One-sided Grubbs’ Test:** We will employ a one-sided Grubbs’ hypothesis test to determine if the performance of $M_{sus}$ is an outlier relative to the expected performance distribution defined by $M_{sdw}$.
    *   **Null Hypothesis ($H_0$):** The mean of $\mathcal{A}_{sus}$ is *not* an outlier (specifically, not significantly lower) compared to $\mathcal{A}_{sdw}$. If $H_0$ holds, the generalization behaviors are similar, implying $M_{sus}$ was trained on data from $G_d$ (Illegal).
    *   **Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$):** The mean of $\mathcal{A}_{sus}$ is a statistically significant low-value outlier. This implies $M_{sus}$ has inferior generalization on our specific synthetic distribution, indicating it was likely trained on a different source (Legal).

We will verify the suspect model based on the rejection or acceptance of $H_0$ at a predefined significance level.

## Expected Contribution
This project aims to deliver the first viable solution for protecting the intellectual property of text-to-image models against "Case 3" infringement (training downstream specific-task models).
1.  **Theoretical Novelty:** We will demonstrate that domain adaptation theory and generalization error bounds can be effectively repurposed for forensic verification in a black-box setting.
2.  **Practical Defense:** We will provide a method that allows defenders to detect IP theft using only their own generative model and API access to the suspect, without needing access to the suspect's training data, weights, or architecture.
3.  **Black-Box Robustness:** By relying on generalization behavior rather than watermarking artifacts, the method is expected to be robust regardless of the specific architecture of the suspect model.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
